title: A Central Nervous System Tumor Mimicking a Lumbar Spine Pathology Causing Acute Foot Drop: A Case Report
case_prompt:
A 53-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with low back pain and acute right foot drop. She had a history of chronic low back pain radiating to both legs for over a year; a lumbar CT performed two months earlier had shown an L5–S1 disc protrusion. She noted an exacerbation of her back pain over the past week and, for the 48 hours before presentation, a sensation of heaviness in her right leg with subjective weakness of dorsiflexion. There was no history of trauma, fever, weight loss, incontinence, or constitutional symptoms.  

Medical history was notable for psoriasis and inflammatory arthritis in remission on sulfasalazine; she was an active smoker (20 pack-years) and worked as a housekeeper.  

On examination, upper-limb strength and reflexes were normal. The left lower limb was normal. In the right lower limb, iliopsoas and quadriceps strength were slightly decreased; tibialis anterior and toe extensor strength were nearly absent. Foot plantar flexors and intrinsic foot muscles were intact. Sensation was reduced over the L5 and S1 dermatomes on the right. The right straight-leg raise test was positive; deep tendon reflexes were normal; plantar responses were flexor. Peripheral pulses were normal.  

Given presumed lumbar radiculopathy, a repeat lumbar CT showed the known central and right L5–S1 disc protrusion with degenerative and sclerotic changes, unchanged from prior imaging. A gadolinium-enhanced lumbar MRI confirmed right L5–S1 foraminal stenosis but showed no central canal stenosis or cord abnormality. A pelvic and hip CT scan was unremarkable for any mass or osseous lesion.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Lumbar radiculopathy was initially favored given chronic back pain and known disc protrusion, but “Since the CT findings did not explain the multi-root pathology noted on physical exam…”  
2. Spinal stenosis was considered for multi-root involvement but “No central spinal stenosis was observed, and the MRI signal suggested normal cord anatomy.”  
3. Inflammatory arthritis was considered as a cause of multi-root neuropathy but “While inflammatory arthritis was a possible explanation for multi-root neuropathy, this is highly unlikely in an arthritis patient in remission.”  
4. Peripheral neuropathy was entertained but “Considering that most neuropathies present with silent foot drop and that no obvious cause for neuropathy was suggested by the history, peripheral neuropathy was not likely.”  
5. A parasagittal brain lesion was then considered because “Parasagittal brain lesion may compress the leg area of the motor cortex and result in an isolated paraparesis.”
